english: One more penalty. If Gonzalo Montiel scores, Argentina becomes world champion.

In the middle of the pitch the captain waits, hugging his teammates. He is thirty-five. He has lost four finals with the national team, and six years ago he said he would leave. This final in Qatar is perhaps his last chance.
As Montiel runs up, the captain looks at the sky. That same sky he points to for his grandmother after almost every goal.
Twenty-five years earlier in Rosario a doctor found that the boy was hardly growing. So every night he stuck a needle into his leg.
Almost four years after the Qatar final, Argentina again played in a World Cup final. Two days later he wrote a short letter. In it were two Spanish words. Me vacié. I emptied myself completely.
He never talked much. He just played. How did a very small, quiet boy carry the weight of a whole country? It all began on a pitch in Rosario, on the day a team was short of a player.
In that letter he also thanked his family. Without them there would be no road for him. The first to believe in him was his grandmother.
It was a small neighbourhood club called Grandoli in Rosario, Argentina. The coach Salvador Aparicio was looking for someone who could play.
At the side of the pitch stood a woman called Celia. She had come to watch her grandson Matías and had brought along his four- or five-year-old younger brother.
She pointed at the little one. The coach hesitated. The boy was very tiny, much smaller than the others. But Celia did not give up. She kept asking him to put the boy on the pitch.
In the end Aparicio agreed. He put the boy on the wing, next to Celia, and said: if he cries, you take him off.
At first he hardly touched the ball. But when the ball came again he took it on his left foot and went round the boys one by one. He did not cry. Years later he remembered scoring two goals that day.
In his first game the boys were two or three years older than him, some almost twice as big. It did not matter.
Aparicio never took him off again. From that day Celia took him to every training session and game.

This boy was Lionel Andrés Messi. He was born on the twenty-fourth of June 1987 in Rosario, the third son of Jorge and Celia. Yes, his mother was also Celia, just like his grandmother. His father worked at a steel factory, his mother in a small workshop making magnets.
He had two older brothers, Rodrigo and Matías. Later his sister María Sol was born and the family was complete.
Rosario is a working city on the Paraná river. Factories, a port, and two clubs that split it in two: Newell's Old Boys and Rosario Central.

The family lived in a simple house in the La Bajada neighbourhood in the south of the city. He played in the street with his brothers until dark. Lionel was always the youngest, and the ball was always with him.
He studied at a state school near his home, school number sixty-six. Years later his face was painted on a wall in the neighbourhood. It says he is from another galaxy and from this neighbourhood.
At home everyone called him Leo. Later, because he was very small and quick, his family and teammates gave him a nickname. La Pulga. The Flea.
According to his mother, at home he was naughty and stubborn. He hated losing even at cards. On the pitch, because of his stubbornness, he never gave up on any ball.
His father and brothers were fans of the red-and-black half of the city, Newell's Old Boys. On match days the family went to the stadium together. Leo already knew where he wanted to play.
At six he came to Newell's Old Boys, the club his family loved. In one of his first games his team won six-nil and he scored four goals.
The boys born in 1987 became a team still remembered in Rosario. They called it "La Máquina del '87", the Machine of '87. For years they almost never lost.
Sometimes opponents would come before the game: if the score reaches six-nil, the game stops. Even at six-nil, if Lionel had not scored himself, he got angry.

Coach Carlos Marconi has told this many times. He promised Leo an alfajor, a chocolate biscuit, for every goal. Leo scored so many that Marconi changed the deal: two alfajores, but only for a headed goal. Soon the smallest boy scored with his head and, smiling at Marconi, showed him two fingers.
His teammates remember small things. Before the game he cleaned his boots and taped his ankles like a professional. He was eight or nine.
One teammate remembers a derby against Rosario Central. Leo fooled one defender again and again, until the defender's father shouted from the stands: kick him.
The league counted his goals. Over two hundred in five years. People in Rosario say the real number is much higher.
His height was always a problem. Big defenders kicked him, some parents shouted: stop him any way you can. Every time he got up and asked for the ball again.
Coaches told him to pass the ball earlier so he would not get injured. But he kept dribbling. If he lost the ball, he won it back at once.
But in 1998, when he was ten, his grandmother Celia died. The person who brought him to football was gone.
Years later he said he loved his grandmother very much, and it is still hard to talk about her. He dedicates his goals to her. After many goals he points to the sky.
According to his mother, after Celia died he talked to his grandmother and asked for help. Few people knew this. He kept his feelings inside.
Without his grandmother he kept playing. He was still the best in the team. But there was another problem, everyone could see it. The other boys were growing, and he was not.
Newell's sent him to the hormone doctor Diego Schwarzstein. The club wanted to know: why is its best young player so small?
The tests showed that Lionel's body lacked growth hormone. Without treatment he would stay ten to fifteen centimetres shorter.
One word followed him for years. Small. The best and the smallest among boys his age in Rosario.
There was a cure: a small injection in the leg every night. But it was very expensive, costing more than nine hundred dollars a month.
As a child he already learned to inject himself. Every night the same: a needle in the leg. A teammate remembers he did it before games as if it was nothing.
His friend's father let him drive a car on a country road. He was eleven.
His father did the sums every month. The medicine took a large part of his factory salary. Insurance and club help did not go far. Without treatment, his son's football would end before it began.
Now they needed a club that would pay. So Lionel went to Buenos Aires for a trial at River Plate, one of the biggest clubs.
In 2026 Messi said this himself. He trained there for about ten days; River wanted to keep him and also pay for his treatment. But first Newell's had to give permission.
He never got that close to a big club in his own country.
But when he went back to Newell's to ask for permission, they said no, and River's offer also went away. It all ended there, he said. Then help came from across the ocean.

An Argentine agent in Barcelona received videos of a boy from Rosario. With a colleague he showed them to the club, and Barcelona invited him for a trial. In September 2000 Lionel flew to Spain with his father. He was thirteen.
At Newell's his teammates did not know where he was. They were told he was ill.
In Barcelona he played with older boys. The sporting director Carles Rexach watched.
They say Rexach could get from his seat to the pitch in three or four minutes. He walked for fifteen minutes: he could not take his eyes off the boy.
Cesc Fàbregas was at the trial; later he played with Messi for years. Before the game the coach told him to mark the new Argentine closely.
Cesc looked at the tiny boy and thought: this will be easy. In a moment Fàbregas was on the ground and the Argentine was gone with the ball.

Later Rexach remembered telling the club: sign him, don't even think about it. But the directors hesitated. The boy was foreign, very small and needed expensive treatment. Weeks passed, nothing was decided.
For Jorge the waiting was terrible. He had left his secure job at the factory. He lived with his son in a hotel in a strange city, not knowing if there would be a home there.
After waiting more than two months, Jorge phoned Rexach and said openly: if this is not decided soon, we go home.
On the fourteenth of December 2000 Rexach met the agents at a tennis club in Barcelona. There was no paper on the table, so he wrote a promise on a napkin: Barcelona will sign Lionel Messi.
Club president Joan Gaspart admitted the napkin had no legal force. It was to calm a father who wanted to leave. And it worked.
Rexach signed, and two agents witnessed it. Years later the napkin sold at auction in London for more than seven hundred and sixty thousand pounds.
Barcelona agreed to pay for the treatment and give his father a job. In February 2001 the family moved to Spain.
Thirteen-year-old Leo did not really understand what all this meant. He only knew he would play and that Barcelona would now pay for the injections.
For the boy from La Bajada it was a dream. For his family it was the start of the hardest year of their lives.
Nothing went as planned. Because of the foreigners rule, Lionel played no official games for months. In only his second game for the youth team he broke his leg.
His mother, brothers and sister missed home. They could not get used to the new city, and in the very first year decided to return to Rosario.
Jorge asked his son: will you come back with us? Lionel said no. Later he put it in one sentence: I wanted to carry on, and my dad stayed with me.
The family was split across two continents. Lionel and his father stayed in Barcelona. Part of Jorge's salary went on life there, the rest to Rosario, to his wife and children.
Now the thirteen-year-old boy was eleven thousand kilometres from his mother, brothers and sister.
On Sundays there was nobody. In a small flat he played video games with his father. According to biographer Guillem Balagué, he then cried into his pillow in his room.
My father was always by my side, Messi said later, we went through many bad days together.
At the club he was silent. At the first training the coach asked: where do you play? He mumbled "forward" and sat down in a corner of the dressing room.
His teammates were puzzled. Fàbregas says for a long time they thought he could not speak. In fact he was very shy. He spoke little. He just played.
They called him "el enano", the dwarf/shorty. But when the ball came, nobody laughed.

Little by little he found his place. In the team there were many born in 1987 like him: Cesc Fàbregas, Gerard Piqué and others. They always attacked with three defenders, and people began calling them the Baby Dream Team.
Bit by bit the quiet boy began to joke. It turned out he was funny and loved cards and video games. In them too, as in football, he hated losing.
In one season they almost never lost; Messi scored over thirty goals. Tall Piqué protected him on the pitch.

Coach Tito Vilanova later became one of the most important people in Messi's life. They say in one game it was three-nil after three minutes. Tito joked to his assistant: if it is eight-nil at half-time, what do we say?
The injections continued every night. Every year he grew a little. By his teens the treatment had done its job.
His height reached about one metre seventy. Still one of the smallest on the pitch. But enough.
Years later his doctor in Rosario, Diego Schwarzstein, said openly: I only helped the boy to grow. Everything else Messi did himself.
In November 2003 Barcelona played at the opening of a new stadium in Porto. Coach Frank Rijkaard brought on sixteen-year-old Lionel Messi from the youth team. On the opposing bench was José Mourinho.
It was only a friendly. But the boy played for the first team. That season he passed through four Barcelona teams in a row.
His official debut was on the sixteenth of October 2004 against Espanyol. He came on near the end, wearing number thirty. He was seventeen.
At the time he was Barcelona's youngest player in the Spanish league. Later that record was broken. He stayed at Barcelona for seventeen years.
At the club they remember: off the pitch he was very shy and silent. One agent had never seen such thin legs on a footballer.
But in the dressing room one person saw it. The best in the world, Ronaldinho, took the quiet boy under his protection.

The Brazilians Deco, Sylvinho, Thiago Motta also looked after the shy teenager. Ronaldinho sat next to him in the dressing room and invited him to the Brazilians' table. Leo says: I learned from all of them, most of all from him.
Not everyone was kind. Frenchman Ludovic Giuly recalls some senior players kicked the boy in training to test what he would do. The boy did not complain, got up and kept playing.
On the first of May 2005 against Albacete Messi came on late. Ronaldinho passed behind the defence, Messi lifted it over the goalkeeper. The referee gave offside.
A few moments later Ronaldinho did exactly the same again. Messi did exactly the same again. This time the goal counted.
Ronaldinho bent down, the boy jumped on his back/shoulders. It was his first official goal for Barcelona. Ronaldinho is proud he was by his side at the start of this story.

Let me pause the story. A word about me. My name is Kamil. I'm twenty-one, and since 2014, since I was nine, I have been starting YouTube channels. Most did not work out. My childhood dream: a hundred thousand subscribers and the silver button. If you like the story, your subscription brings me one step closer. Now back to the story.
In spring 2006, in the Champions League knockout stage, Messi bewildered Chelsea at Stamford Bridge. Two weeks later, in the return game, he tore a thigh muscle and went off crying.
The whole Camp Nou stood and applauded. Rijkaard hugged him. Messi was eighteen.
Barcelona won the final in Paris. Messi did not play. He was so upset he did not join the celebration. Years later he said he deeply regrets that night.
In 2004 a new question had arisen. Messi had lived in Spain since he was thirteen. Spain was inviting him to its national team.
Argentina's youth coaches hurried. In June 2004 the under-20s played a friendly against Paraguay. The aim: to tie Messi to his country.
Argentina won eight-nil. Messi said playing for Spain had really been possible. But in his heart he was from Rosario.

His friend from the academy, Cesc Fàbregas, said it would have been great if Leo had played for Spain. A few years later Spain won the World Cup without him. Argentina waited another eleven years for the trophy.
In 2005 at the youth World Cup in the Netherlands he was the best player. He scored six goals, including two penalties in the final against Nigeria. Argentina became world champion.
He received the best player of the tournament award and the top scorer's Golden Boot. The boy from Rosario became champion in the white-and-sky-blue shirt for the first time.
Six weeks later, in August 2005, he debuted for the national team in a friendly against Hungary in Budapest. He came on in the second half.

At his first touch a defender pulled his shirt. Messi swung his arm trying to get free, and it hit the defender. The referee showed a red card. Not even a minute had passed. They say he went off crying.
Later he said what he thought: I came on, they sent me off, now they'll never call me up again.
One of his teammates ran to argue with the referee for him. His name is Lionel Scaloni. Remember this name, he will come back in this story.
They called him up again. In March 2006 he scored his first goal for Argentina against Croatia. In summer he went to his first World Cup in Germany.
Coming off the bench against Serbia and Montenegro, he scored the sixth goal. At eighteen he became the youngest Argentine to score at a World Cup.
That day he also set up a goal for Hernán Crespo. He already belonged there.
In the quarter-final Argentina was ahead of hosts Germany. The coach used the last substitution on others, the game slipped away. They lost on penalties.
Messi spent the whole game on the bench. A World Cup ended for the first time while he watched. He said nothing to journalists. Again he spoke little.
In April 2007, in the Spanish Cup semi-final against Getafe, Messi got the ball in his own half. He went round one player, another, another, and the goalkeeper too, and scored.
He started on the right, at the halfway line. In ten seconds, ball glued to his left foot, he almost crossed the whole pitch.
Everyone in Argentina recognised this goal. Their greatest hero Diego Maradona had scored almost exactly the same goal against England at the 1986 World Cup. Messi was nineteen.
Barcelona won five-two. But in the return game Getafe won four-nil and Barcelona went out. Even such a goal did not save the team.
These were hard years for Barcelona. Ronaldinho was fading, the team was losing, the club was looking for renewal. Messi grew stronger month by month but was often injured.
In the letter he wrote after the 2026 final there is another line: I swear I always gave everything. It was true. But for many years, with Argentina, everything was not enough to win.
In summer 2007, in the Copa América final in Venezuela, Argentina played Brazil. He had just turned twenty. Brazil won three-nil.
He played ninety minutes and could do almost nothing. In the end he watched Brazil celebrate.
This was his first final with the national team. Nobody knew: before winning one, he would lose three more.
In 2008 he wanted to play at the Beijing Olympics. Barcelona would not release him, because the Games were not in the official football calendar. The case went to a special sports court.
Messi said: the decision is mine, I will never get another chance to play at the Olympics. The court sided with the clubs.
But the new coach Pep Guardiola had won Olympic gold in Barcelona in 1992. He understood and released Messi.
At the Games he scored against Ivory Coast and the Netherlands.

In the final against Nigeria, in front of about ninety thousand spectators, after his pass his friend Ángel Di María lifted the ball over the goalkeeper. It was the only goal. Argentina won Olympic gold.

He said in football some things happen once in a lifetime. It was his only Olympics. He calls the gold one of his most precious wins. Meanwhile in Barcelona Guardiola was preparing a new role for him.
Guardiola's first decision was unexpected. He told Messi's hero Ronaldinho: you are not in my plans. The team would now be built around a twenty-one-year-old.
That summer Ronaldinho left for Milan. As he left he told Leo: take my number ten. The quiet boy who once jumped on his back now wore his number and was the team's star.
In May 2009 Barcelona played Real Madrid at the Bernabéu. According to journalist Martí Perarnau, the evening before Guardiola called Messi to his room and showed him a video.
There was a gap between Real's midfield and defence. Guardiola said: start on the right, then move to the middle, into the gap. When the ball comes, run at goal.
According to the book, Guardiola kept the plan secret until the last moment.
Messi played neither on the wing nor up front. He was in between, and the defenders did not know who should mark him. Barcelona won six-two in Madrid. Messi scored two.
Days later, in the semi-final at Stamford Bridge, Barcelona was losing in the ninety-third minute. Messi passed, Andrés Iniesta scored. Barcelona in the final!
Three weeks later, the Champions League final in Rome. The opponent: Manchester United. Before the game Guardiola showed a season video with the music of "Gladiator".
Before the final Leo remembered Paris: the night he felt left out and did not join the celebration. This time, he said, I must enjoy it more.
In the seventieth minute Xavi crossed. The smallest player jumped high and headed it over goalkeeper Edwin van der Sar.
Van der Sar was nearly two metres. Messi was about one metre seventy. The little boy beat him in the air.
Barcelona won two-nil.
That year they won every trophy. The league, the cup, the Champions League and three more. Six out of six. No team had ever done this.
The sixth was in December in Abu Dhabi, against Argentina's Estudiantes. In extra time Messi scored the winning goal with his chest.
Weeks earlier he had received his first Ballon d'Or, the award for the world's best footballer. He was twenty-two. The little boy was now the best.
In January 2011 the Ballon d'Or was presented in Zurich. All three finalists came from one school, Barcelona's academy La Masia: Xavi, Andrés Iniesta and Lionel Messi.
Many thought Xavi or Iniesta would win. They were from world champions Spain, and Iniesta had scored the final goal. But Messi won for the second time in a row.
Leo said he had not expected it. He said Xavi and Iniesta deserved it as much as he did, maybe more. They were the first to congratulate him.
The three held a press conference together and said the same thing. The award belonged to the team.
Years later Xavi recalled meeting him on a trip: a polite, modest boy without arrogance. He had not thought this boy would become the greatest footballer in history.

In May 2011 at Wembley Barcelona beat Manchester United again in the Champions League final. Messi scored with a powerful low shot from distance. The most moving moment came at the end. That spring defender Éric Abidal had a tumour removed from his liver. Carles Puyol gave the captain's armband to Abidal so that he could lift the trophy.

In May 2012 Guardiola led Barcelona in his last home game. Messi scored all four goals. After the fourth he ran to the side and hugged him. Guardiola said: Leo drew all the attention all season, I can't even be jealous.
In December 2012 he broke a forty-year-old record. Gerd Müller had scored eighty-five goals in one calendar year. Messi scored ninety-one that year, five of them in one Champions League game.

Müller was not hurt. He called Leo a giant and joked: his only fault is that he doesn't play for Bayern. A few weeks later Leo sent him a Barcelona shirt. On it was handwritten: with respect and admiration, a hug. Leo said trophies are more important than records.
His life outside football changed too. His girlfriend was Antonela Roccuzzo, a girl from Rosario he had known since childhood. In November 2012 their first son Thiago was born.
Two months after Thiago was born, Leo said: becoming a father changes you completely. Now his son was most important of all.

In January 2013 he received his fourth Ballon d'Or in a row. Nobody had won it four times. But that winter Tito Vilanova was again being treated for cancer. He was that coach from La Masia, now head of the first team. And Abidal had come back after a liver transplant. In his speech in Zurich Leo forgot to thank them, and later apologised. Leo had said: Tito believed in him already when he was a boy sitting on the bench.
At Barcelona he was a living legend. In the national team it was different.
Argentina had not won a major trophy since 1993, since Messi was six. Now the whole nation believed he would end this wait.

At the 2010 World Cup in South Africa Diego Maradona himself coached Argentina. In the quarter-final in Cape Town Germany scored in the third minute and won four-nil. Messi did not score a single goal in the tournament.
After the game Maradona said: I saw Messi crying in the room.
And those who say he doesn't care about this shirt are fools, he said.
Because in Argentina many people said exactly that. He had gone to Spain at thirteen. He had never played for an Argentine club. Before games he didn't even sing the anthem.
Such a footballer they called "pecho frío". That is, cold chest. Someone who doesn't feel enough at important moments. For many his silence was indifference.
At the 2011 Copa América in his own country, fans whistled at him. His father said: my son was very hurt, he didn't understand why.

At that tournament coach Sergio Batista tried to make him play like at Barcelona. It didn't work. Messi said: comparing Argentina with Barcelona is a mistake. Barcelona is a team that has played together for years.
Argentina lost to Uruguay on penalties in the quarter-final. At home the criticism did not stop. Then he did as always. He didn't talk much. He just played.

In April 2014 Tito Vilanova died at the age of forty-five. His former assistant says that six days earlier Leo had visited him at home and they talked for hours. The coach of Leo's first great team was gone.

Less than two months later, at the World Cup in Brazil, Messi pulled the team forward. After his first goal, against Bosnia, he looked to the sky as usual. He scored four goals in the group. Against Iran he scored the winner in the ninety-first minute.
He was man of the match four times. Argentina reached the world final for the first time in twenty-four years.
In the semi-final the Netherlands were beaten on penalties. Defender Javier Mascherano said: without Leo Argentina would not have got here.
The final was at the Maracanã in Rio de Janeiro, again against Germany. Messi and his teammates had chances. No goal. In extra time Mario Götze scored.
After the game Messi was given the best player of the tournament award. Going to collect it, he walked past the World Cup trophy without looking at it.
He said this award did not interest him. Then-FIFA president Sepp Blatter later said Messi kept repeating to himself: the best, but not the champion.
It was the second lost final. Three years later he said: this pain stays for a lifetime.
At the 2015 Copa América in Chile Argentina reached the final again. After one hundred and twenty minutes against Chile it was nil-nil. Messi scored his penalty. Two teammates missed, and Chile won.
A month before the final he had won the Champions League again with Barcelona in Berlin, with Neymar and Luis Suárez. At the club he won everything; with the national team he lost.
In the final Chile's coach was the Argentine Jorge Sampaoli. Two years later he would coach Argentina.
After the final Messi wrote: in football nothing is harder than losing a final. He had now lost three finals.
In June 2016 there was another chance. A special Copa América was held in the USA, a hundred years after the first. The final was at MetLife Stadium near New York.
The opponent was Chile again. Again no one scored. Again it came down to a penalty shoot-out.
Messi took the first penalty. He leaned back, the ball flew over the goal.
Chile won. It was his fourth lost final with Argentina. Three in a row in three years.
Lucas Biglia's shot was also saved. But everyone remembered the captain's mistake.
Minutes later a journalist stopped him in the tunnel. The quiet man said a few words: that's it, the national team is over for me.
His teammates were crushed. Sergio Agüero was his closest friend. For years they shared a room at almost every camp. Agüero said: the defeat broke Leo.
Messi cried on his shoulder for about twenty-five seconds like a little boy, repeating: this is not for me, this is not for me.
The fitness coach says that at two in the morning that night Leo was still awake, crying.

Then something unexpected happened. In Argentina people began asking him to stay. The president phoned him and said openly that Messi is Argentina's greatest treasure. On a rainy Saturday hundreds of people came to the Obelisk in Buenos Aires with signs. "Don't go, Leo."
In a corner of Argentina, fifteen-year-old Enzo Fernández also wrote him a letter asking him not to go. Six years later that boy played with him in a world final.
The country that had called him cold now wanted him back. Less than two months later he announced his return. In his first game back he scored.
They asked why he came back. He said: I love my country and this shirt very much, I want to help.
Then he gave the reason he left: not only the pain of defeat; things outside football had also hurt him and his family.
He couldn't even remember telling his father before speaking in the tunnel. At that moment it felt like that was how it had to be, he said.
That summer a Spanish court found Messi and his father guilty of tax fraud over image rights. The prison sentence was changed to a fine; for a first offence this is normal.
In court Messi said his father handled the money matters. The family had by then paid back about five million euros.

In June 2017 Leo married Antonela in Rosario, the city where they grew up. He could have had the wedding anywhere, but he chose home. About two hundred and fifty guests came, including teammates from Barcelona and Argentina. Thiago and his younger brother Mateo sat in the front row; his brothers and sister signed as witnesses.
On the pitch Argentina struggled. Until the last game of 2018 World Cup qualifying it was not in a qualifying spot. It had to win in Quito, high in the Andes. It had not won there for sixteen years.

That night Argentina's streets were almost empty. People watched in cafés and at home. In La Plata the band U2 even delayed their concert so fans could watch the game on a big screen. In the first minute Ecuador scored, and the cafés fell silent.
Then Messi scored three goals. Argentina won three-one and set off for Russia. Even Ecuador's fans applauded.
In the dressing room they sang a song aimed at the critics. Mascherano said: if we hadn't qualified, many of us would have been finished.
Messi said later: Argentina not being at the World Cup would have been madness. Now we're calm.
Sampaoli's words were remembered: Messi doesn't owe Argentina a World Cup. Football owes Messi a World Cup.
Russia did not pay the debt. In the first game against Iceland Messi missed a penalty.
The goalkeeper who saved it, Hannes Halldórsson, was also a film director. He had studied Messi's penalties in advance.
Then they lost three-nil to Croatia. They beat Nigeria with a Messi goal, which he called a great relief.
In Kazan, for the round of sixteen against France, Antonela, Thiago and Mateo came. The boys wore shirts that said Papá. Argentina lost four-three. Messi again went home empty-handed.

In his 2026 farewell letter he wrote again: the decision to leave the national team hurt his heart deeply and still hurts. He felt this pain at Barcelona too. There the end began with European nights no one at the club wants to remember.

Things had started to go wrong. In 2018, after easily beating Roma in the first game, they lost three-nil in Rome. A year later the same again: they beat Liverpool three-nil at home and lost four-nil in Liverpool.
A few days after Anfield he said the coach was not to blame. Much of the blame was his and his teammates'.
In 2019 he received his sixth Ballon d'Or, the most in history. But it did not stop the decline around him.
And in August 2020 in Lisbon Bayern beat Barcelona eight-two.
Ten days after Lisbon Messi sent the club an official letter: he wanted to leave. Barcelona refused: the contract does not allow it.
His father flew to Barcelona to talk with the club. In the end Messi said he would stay one more year: he would not take the club he loves to court.
Six weeks after Lisbon, the club sent away one of his closest friends, Luis Suárez. Leo wrote: Suárez deserved a proper farewell, not being thrown out like this. Nothing surprises me anymore.
In November 2020 Diego Maradona died. Argentina mourned for days. The man who had defended Messi after Cape Town was gone, and the country had still not won a big trophy with Messi.
That year the world was in lockdown because of the pandemic. In summer 2021 the Copa América was moved to Brazil at the last minute. The final at the Maracanã against Brazil.
Because of the pandemic there were almost no fans in the stadium. One of his biggest games with Argentina would take place in silence.
The players had been away from their families for weeks. Before the final, in the room, the quiet captain stood up. Someone filmed it.
For years people said he was too quiet to lead. That night he found his voice.

Forty-five days we haven't seen our families, guys, he said. He reminded them that goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez had become a father and had not yet held his little daughter. And he finished: we go out with confidence and calm, and we take this cup home.
Afterwards Martínez said he felt like crying. Another player burst into tears at once and doesn't remember the rest.
In the twenty-second minute Rodrigo De Paul played a long pass. It was taken by Ángel Di María, the friend Messi passed to for Olympic gold. He lifted the ball over the goalkeeper. One-nil.
For the next seventy minutes Brazil attacked and Argentina held on. Messi couldn't score a second. It didn't matter.
At the final whistle Messi knelt and covered his face with his hands. His teammates ran and jumped on top of him, and he disappeared from view.
Then he called his wife and sons in Rosario. After losing four finals, he finally won a trophy with the national team. He was thirty-four.
Later Di María said: the bad luck had to end one day, and finally it has. Messi dedicated the win to his family, to the Argentine people, and to Maradona: wherever he is, he must be cheering for us.
A month later a new contract was to be signed. But the club said that because of debt and Spanish league rules it could not keep him.
On the eighth of August 2021 he entered a room at Camp Nou to say goodbye. Before saying a word, he burst into tears.
He was not ready for this. He wanted to stay with his family. He came to this city at thirteen and was leaving at thirty-four with three sons: Thiago, Mateo and Ciro, all born here.
It was also hard that he could not say goodbye to fans in the stadium. Because of the pandemic he hadn't seen them for a year and a half.
He moved to Paris Saint-Germain. It didn't go well. When they lost, they whistled at him.
Once after a defeat he flew to Saudi Arabia on an advertising trip without the club's permission. Paris suspended him and he apologised in a video. Everyone knew he would not stay.

In November 2022 Argentina arrived at the Qatar World Cup unbeaten in thirty-six games. The coach was Lionel Scaloni, the teammate who defended Messi in Budapest. Messi was thirty-five. Everyone knew: this was probably the last chance.
In the first game he scored a penalty against Saudi Arabia. Then the opponents scored two goals in five minutes: two-one. It was one of the biggest shocks in World Cup history.
After the game Messi faced the press. No excuses, he said. The dressing room was silent. But he asked the Argentine people to believe in the team: we will be more united than ever.
In the following days he talked a lot, the team says. The quiet captain now led openly.
One song followed them. The fans called it Muchachos. The team sang it on the bus, in the room, Messi too.
Now every game was a final. Against Mexico Messi scored the first goal, two-nil. Then they beat Poland and Australia.
Against Australia he played his thousandth game and scored.
In the quarter-final Argentina was two-nil up against Holland, but the opponents equalised in the last seconds. Argentina won on penalties.
After that the world saw a new Messi. During an interview a Dutchman walked past. Messi said to him in the language of Rosario's streets: "What are you looking at, fool?"

The player called cold was now on fire. In the semi-final Argentina beat Croatia three-nil. Messi scored a penalty, then dribbled past one of the best young defenders and set up a goal for Julián Álvarez.
The eighteenth of December 2022, the final. Argentina and France. Messi scored a penalty. Di María scored the second.
Two-nil. Ten minutes left. Four lost finals behind, and the trophy right beside him.
Then in less than two minutes Kylian Mbappé scored two goals. Two-two.
Extra time. Messi scored again. Three-two. Then Mbappé scored again, from a penalty. Three-three.
In the last minute Martínez saved another French shot with his foot. One hundred and twenty minutes passed. Decisive penalties.
Messi scored. Martínez saved one, France missed another. Montiel's turn, the decisive kick.
This is that moment from the start of the film. Montiel walked up to the ball. Messi looked to the sky. He later said he asked God to let it end.
Montiel scored. Lionel Messi knelt on the grass.
He had lost four finals with Argentina. He had said: it's over. He came back. And now, at thirty-five, he is world champion.
Before the trophy the Emir of Qatar put a traditional black robe over his shoulders. Then he lifted the trophy, kissed it, and did not let go.
Then his family came onto the pitch. His mother hugged him. His three sons ran over. He took a photo of Antonela with the trophy.

In the final he scored his sixth and seventh goals of the tournament. He was again given the best player award. The award he did not value eight years earlier because he had lost. Now he had the trophy too.
At that tournament he became the first player to score in the group, round of sixteen, quarter-final, semi-final and final.
Later in a TV interview he said the trophy called to him, as if saying: now you may touch me.
He hasn't watched the final again, only highlights, he says. At home his sons celebrate imitating goalkeeper Martínez.
In Buenos Aires millions of people came out into the streets. There were so many that the bus could not move, and the players were taken away by helicopter.

In March 2023, before leaving Europe, there was another happy night in Buenos Aires. In his first home game as champion, at the Monumental against Panama, he scored his eight hundredth goal. I always dreamed of this moment, he said: celebrating with my people, at home.
That summer, when his Paris contract ended, he surprised everyone. Not Barcelona. Not the huge Saudi offer either. A young club in the USA, Inter Miami. Many thought he was going there to rest.
He explained simply. He wanted to step a little away from fame and spend more time with his family. If it were about money, I'd have gone to Saudi Arabia, he said.
July 2023, the first game in Miami. He came on in the second half. In the ninety-fourth minute, at one-one, he curled a free kick into the corner.
On that first night he smiled from the bench at Antonela and his three sons in the stands. LeBron James and Serena Williams had come too. When the goal went in, club co-owner David Beckham cried.
A few weeks later Miami won its first trophy. So much for resting. In October he received his eighth Ballon d'Or.
In Miami he also became a football dad. His three sons attended the club academy. He and Antonela stood at the side like ordinary parents, supporting them.
In 2024 Argentina again played in the Copa América final, in Miami, against Colombia. In the second half his ankle gave way and he was substituted.

On the bench he cried. Leandro Paredes sat next to him. I couldn't look at him, I only heard him crying, says Paredes. Argentina won in extra time without him. It was also the last game for his friend Di María.

In September 2025, as he himself said, he played probably his last qualifier at home: in Buenos Aires against Venezuela. During the warm-up he barely held back tears, while more than eighty thousand people chanted his name. He scored two goals. My dream was to finish like this at home, he said.
In December 2025 Miami won the MLS Cup for the first time. On the pitch his son Mateo played with the ball, then pointed at his father.
In March 2026 he scored his nine hundredth goal. He was thirty-eight; some said he was too old.
The goal came in a game Miami did not win and went out of a continental cup. For him the result matters more than the record. Ahead lay one more World Cup.
His father Jorge always wanted to see him at one more World Cup. But before the tournament Jorge fell seriously ill. For the first time Jorge could not watch him.
In the first game he scored three against Algeria. Then two against Austria, one against Jordan. Argentina easily topped the group.
After every game the same. Boots come off. Phone is taken. Any news from home? That was how he learned how his father was.
He didn't say it then, but his father was ill thousands of kilometres away. Later he admitted he did not feel well at all during the whole tournament.
In the knockout stage every game was a battle. Against Cape Verde there was extra time.
Against Egypt he missed a penalty but did not break. He set up a goal for Cristian Romero, equalised himself, and Enzo Fernández headed the winner. Against Switzerland, extra time again.
Boots. Phone. Any news from home?

In the semi-final, in Atlanta, the opponent was England. England went ahead. Argentina turned the game in the last five minutes, and in the last minute Messi lifted in the winning goal. Two-one. Another final!
After the whistle Messi was overcome with emotion. Then he went round the pitch hugging the team and staff. Coach Scaloni was also lost for words.
He scored eight goals at that World Cup. No one has scored more goals or played more games at World Cups than him.
The final was on the nineteenth of July 2026 at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. Exactly here, ten years earlier, he had said it was all over.
Before the game he told the team to be calm, forget everything and think only about the game.
Spain had nineteen-year-old Lamine Yamal and a team full of young players. The ball and the chances were theirs.
The score was still nil-nil. In a video released later Messi tells his team: show character, everyone, character!
At the end of normal time Enzo Fernández, that boy who had written him a letter, was sent off. Ten men, thirty minutes to hold on.
In the hundred and sixth minute Ferran Torres scored. Argentina could not respond.
Messi had one shot in the whole game. It was his fifth lost final.

After the whistle Messi sat on the grass. Yamal came and hugged him. Messi told him: follow your own path, the future belongs to your generation. Yamal said these words were as precious as a gold medal.
Scaloni cried at the press conference and walked out. Before the final he had called Messi the greatest footballer who ever stepped on a pitch.
The next day Messi wrote to the fans: the pain is endless, and this wound will need time to heal.
Less than three weeks after the final, in August 2026, Jorge Messi died in Rosario after a long illness. He was sixty-eight.
A few days later Lionel wrote him a letter and shared it with the world. The letter began simply: I love you, Dad.

He had promised his father: we'll reach the final, you'll come and watch. His father couldn't make it. Lionel wanted to win the cup and bring it to his father. But I couldn't, he wrote. There was no strength left in my legs.
He also wrote that during the tournament he waited for news of his father after every game. When no news came, he understood how bad things were.
You were my father, my friend and my agent, he wrote. The man who left his job in Rosario and waited for a napkin in Barcelona.
Now when he looked at the sky, there were two people up there.
On the thirty-first of August he posted the letter from the start of the film. He had written it on the twenty-first of July, two days after the final, and kept it for six weeks.
In it he said goodbye to the national team. Me vacié, he wrote. I emptied myself completely. I have nothing left to give; great young players worthy of the place are coming. Now I'm one of you too.
Later he added one sentence at the end: today, after what happened to my dad, I am even more sure of my decision.
He did not write about trophies or finals. He wrote about his family, the fans and his father.

On the sixth of October 2026 he played for Argentina for the last time: a friendly against Benin at the Monumental. That is River Plate's stadium in Buenos Aires. The club that once wanted the little boy from Rosario but could not get him.
Nearly eighty-five thousand people came. He came out holding his three sons' hands. His mother watched from the stands.
The anthem was sung by a Falklands War veteran. Messi barely held back tears. In the tenth minute the game stopped for a long ovation, and the Benin players came over to him.
He set up two goals, then scored a penalty. His hundred and twenty-sixth goal for Argentina in his two hundred and eighth game.
From the second assist, twenty-two-year-old Nico Paz scored, one of the young players he called worthy of the place.
Then hundreds of drones lit up the sky over the stadium. The boy who once sat silent in a corner of the dressing room took the microphone in front of eighty-five thousand people.
First he said he was thinking of his father. Then that this was the saddest day of his career.
For weeks there had been arguments about the tournament's referees. Messi stayed out of it. That night he said nothing strange happened. His team gave everything.
Playing for Argentina is the most beautiful happiness, he said. I wanted to be here all my life. Then he told the fans he loves them and will miss them.
He went round the pitch with his wife and three sons, as eighty-five thousand people sang that Messi isn't leaving.
He had called it the saddest day of his career. But in his letter he had written: I leave with peace and pride.
He was too small. Too expensive. A stranger in Spain, unknown in Argentina. And then they said he was too old.
But two people didn't believe that. The grandmother who told the coach: let him play. The father who found the money, crossed the ocean and stayed by his side.
He didn't play only for himself. He played for them. After a goal, looking to the sky, it is them he looks for.
The cold chest Argentina talked about was not cold at all. He just didn't show his feelings. He kept them inside and let them out only when he lost or when he finally won.
The last final, in July 2026, was the most painful. It wasn't about the trophy. It was the last gift he wanted to bring to his father.
Today he still plays in Miami. He has scored more than nine hundred goals. He no longer plays for Argentina. As he himself wrote, he is now just a fan.
Maybe you are quiet too. The child in the corner of the room. The one everyone calls indifferent.

Leo was that kind of child too. He did not become a loud person. He didn't talk much. He played for those who believed in him. And at the most important moment he found his voice. One day the whole world listened.
Are you quiet? You don't have to speak loudly. Just keep playing. Your time to speak will come.
On the night he said goodbye to Argentina, the boy who barely spoke smiled at eighty-five thousand people. I'm talking more than ever, he said, I don't want to leave.
That summer Spain did not only end Leo's last World Cup. Two weeks earlier in Texas it had also broken the dream of another boy who wanted the trophy so badly.
He is from a small island in the Atlantic. His teammates once called him a crybaby. His name is Cristiano Ronaldo, and his full story is right here.
